verdict.rationale: Romans 5:12-19 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49 build a tightly structured one-and-many parallel between Adam and Christ. The Greek repeats 'through one man' (di' henos anthropou) against 'the many' (hoi polloi), binds the two halves with 'just as' (hosper, G5618) and 'so also' (houtos, G3779), names Adam 'a type of the one to come' (typos tou mellontos, with typos meaning pattern or model, G5179) in 5:14, and frames 1 Corinthians 15:22 with the incorporative 'in' (en, G1722) plus dative (the 'to/in X' grammatical form), 'in Adam all die' (en to Adam pantes apothneskousin) set against 'in Christ' (en to Christo). The text therefore plainly establishes Adam as a representative whose one act has corporate consequence and as the counterpart head to Christ. What the vocabulary does NOT do is name the mechanism. It never calls Adam a covenant or federal head, and Paul's technical reckoning verb 'to credit or count' (logizomai, G3049), which saturates Romans 4, is absent from the Adam passage. The crux phrase 'because/in whom all sinned' (eph' ho pantes hemarton) in 5:12 carries both 'on/upon' (epi, G1909) and the relative pronoun 'who/whom' (hos, G3739), so it reads either causally (because all sinned) or relatively (in whom all sinned). The same data fit a federal, a seminal, and an influence-analogy account, so the structural claim is supported but the specific federal-imputation form is disputed.

scripture.force: Token query of Romans 5:12 returns the chain 'through one man' (di' henos anthropou, that is G1223 plus G1520 plus G0444), 'sin' (hamartia, G0266), 'into the world' (eis ton kosmon, G1519 plus G2889), and 'so' (houtos, G3779) introducing 'to all men' (eis pantas anthropous) death came. The closing clause 'because/in whom all sinned' (eph' ho pantes hemarton) contains BOTH 'on/upon' (epi, G1909) and the relative pronoun 'who/whom' (hos, G3739), confirmed in the queried token sequence. That dual morphology, the way one short phrase carries two possible grammatical readings, is the heart of the dispute. Read as 'on/upon' plus relative pronoun causally, the phrase means 'because all sinned', grounding universal death in each person's own sinning. With 'one man' (henos anthropou) as the antecedent of 'who/whom' (hos) it reads 'in whom all sinned', grounding death in corporate inclusion in the one man. The Greek supplies both possibilities and does not rank them. The one-to-many transmission is explicit, the mechanism is not.

'But sin is not charged where there is no law' (hamartia de ouk ellogeitai me ontos nomou), that is sin is not 'reckoned' or 'charged to an account' (ellogeo, G1677) where there is no law. The verb 'to charge to an account' (ellogeo) occurs only twice in the canon (here and Philemon 18), so its sense as 'charge to an account' is set by the commercial Philemon usage, not triangulated from a wide field. Paired with verse 14, that death nonetheless reigned from Adam to Moses, it signals that the death of those between Adam and Moses cannot be charged purely to their own statutory violations (their own breaking of written law) and must trace back to Adam's act. This favors a corporate or representative reading but does not by itself isolate federal imputation (the appointed-legal-representative form, where Adam's guilt is legally credited to his people) from seminal participation (the everyone-was-naturally-in-Adam form) or inherited mortality.

'Death reigned' (ebasileusen ho thanatos) from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in 'the likeness' (homoioma, G3667) of Adam's transgression. This is the strongest single-verse hint that the death pronounced on Adam reaches descendants apart from their own Adam-like statutory violation (their own breaking of a clear command). Paul then names Adam 'a type of the coming one' (typos tou mellontos), using 'type, pattern' (typos, G5179), a term that elsewhere means pattern, model, or example (1 Peter 5:3, Philippians 3:17, 1 Corinthians 10:6, with 15 occurrences in the New Testament canon). The word 'type, pattern' (typos) formalizes the Adam-to-Christ correspondence as an analogical type, which is why one defensible reading treats the whole comparison as a representative analogy rather than a juridical transfer (a courtroom-style transfer of guilt).

'By the trespass of the one the many died' (to tou henos paraptomati hoi polloi apethanon). The word 'trespass' (paraptoma, G3900) occurs 21 times in the canon and clusters densely in Romans 5 (verses 15, 16, 17, 18, 20), confirming it is the controlling term for Adam's act in this paragraph. It is paired with the gift in grace by the one man Jesus Christ abounding to the many, the contrast qualified by 'so much more' (pollo mallon), asserting asymmetric superiority of the gift over the trespass.

'Judgment from one issuing in condemnation' (krima ex henos eis katakrima), set against 'gift from many trespasses issuing in righteous verdict' (charisma ek pollon paraptomaton eis dikaioma). The word 'condemnation' (katakrima, G2631) occurs only 3 times in the canon, all in Romans (5:16, 5:18, 8:1), so it is a narrow Pauline forensic (courtroom-style) term. The judicial register of 'judgment' (krima), 'condemnation' (katakrima), and 'righteous verdict or requirement' (dikaioma, G1345) is the strongest lexical support for understanding the one-to-many transmission in a legal frame, though 'from one' (ex henos) is itself ambiguous between 'one trespass' and 'one man'.

'Through one trespass to all men for condemnation, so also through one righteous act to all men for justification of life' (di' henos paraptomatos eis pantas anthropous eis katakrima, houtos kai di' henos dikaiomatos eis pantas anthropous eis dikaiosin zoes). The strict parallel runs 'through one trespass to all men for condemnation, so through one righteous act to all men for justification of life'. The same preposition 'into/for' (eis) carries the result both times, anchoring a symmetric one-to-all flow. The verse states the scope (to all) and the channel (through one) but does not encode whether the channel is covenantal appointment, natural descent, or analogy.

Token query confirms 'to constitute or appoint' (kathistemi, G2525) occurs TWICE in this verse, 'the many were constituted sinners' (hamartoloi katestathesan hoi polloi) by the 'disobedience' (parakoe, G3876) of the one, and 'will be constituted righteous' (dikaioi katastathesontai) by the 'obedience' (hypakoe, G5218) of the one. The verb 'to constitute, appoint' (kathistemi) occurs 22 times in the canon and its dominant attested sense is to appoint or set in office or place ('set over the household' Matthew 24:45, 'appoint' Acts 6:3, 'appoint elders' Titus 1:5). That 'appoint' or 'constitute-into-a-status' nuance is the closest the Greek comes to status-conferral language (wording that places someone into a category by official designation). It is genuine but not the technical reckoning verb 'to credit or count' (logizomai, G3049) which Paul uses 11 times across Romans 4 and never here, so 'to constitute' (kathistemi) underdetermines whether the constituting is forensic imputation (legal crediting in a courtroom frame) or realistic incorporation (actual ontological union with Adam).

'For since through a man came death, also through a man resurrection of the dead' (epeide gar di' anthropou thanatos, kai di' anthropou anastasis nekron). The 'through' (dia) plus genitive of agent (the 'by-means-of-X' grammatical form) restates the channel from one human to a consequence reaching others, applied first to Adam (implied) and then to Christ. It establishes paired human agency without naming the basis on which the one man's act binds others.

'For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive' (hosper gar en to Adam pantes apothneskousin, houtos kai en to Christo pantes zoopoiethesontai). Token query confirms 'in' (en, G1722) appears TWICE, once with Adam and once with Christ, framed by 'just as' (hosper, G5618) and 'so also' (houtos, G3779). The incorporative 'in' (en) plus dative (the 'to/in X' grammatical form), 'in Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive', is the clearest pan-NT (spread across the whole New Testament) statement of corporate solidarity in Adam and it is exactly symmetric with solidarity in Christ. The phrase makes the two-head corporate pattern explicit. It does not, by itself, adjudicate between forensic imputation (legal crediting), seminal-realist inclusion (everyone really present in Adam by nature), and representative analogy, because 'in' (en) plus dative is a locative-incorporative idiom (a 'placed inside or united with' figure of speech) that all three readings can claim.

'The first man Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit' (ho protos anthropos Adam eis psychen zosan, ho eschatos Adam eis pneuma zoopoioun). Token query confirms 'Adam' (Adam, G0076) appears twice in the verse with 'last' (eschatos). Calling Christ the last Adam formally constitutes Adam and Christ as the paired representative men of two humanities. The 'genitive of source' (a noun in the 'from-X' grammatical form, indicating where something comes from) from Genesis 2:7 is reused for Adam and extended to Christ as 'life-giving spirit'. This is the lexical hinge that turns a single typological comparison into a two-representative framework.

'The first man from earth, dusty, the second man from heaven' (ho protos anthropos ek ges choikos, ho deuteros anthropos ex ouranou). The first man from earth, 'dusty, made of dust' (choikos, G5517, a 4-occurrence term confined to this passage, verses 47, 48, 49), the second man from heaven. The numbering 'first' (protos) and 'second' (deuteros) formalizes the two-head structure and underlines that the contrast is between two persons who stand for two orders of humanity.

'Just as we bore the image of the dusty one, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly one' (kathos ephoresamen ten eikona tou choikou, phoresomen kai ten eikona tou epouraniou). Bearing the 'image, likeness' (eikon, G1504) of the 'dusty one' (choikos) and the image of the 'heavenly one' (epouranios, G2032). The 'image' (eikon) language of corporate likeness ties each set of people to their respective head, reinforcing the representative pattern by likeness rather than by an explicit covenant or legal term.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase 'because/in whom all sinned' (eph' ho pantes hemarton) is the central complicating sub-clause and the token query confirms it is built from 'on/upon' (epi, G1909) plus the relative pronoun 'who/whom' (hos, G3739). Read causally, 'because all sinned', it grounds death in each person's actual sinning and weakens a strict imputation (legal-crediting) reading. Read as a relative phrase with 'one man' (henos anthropou) as antecedent, 'in whom all sinned', it grounds death in corporate inclusion in Adam. Greek vocabulary and grammar permit both and Romans 5:13-14, death from Adam to Moses without statutory law (without an explicit written commandment), immediately tensions the purely causal reading. Decisively for neutrality, Paul does NOT deploy his technical reckoning verb 'to credit or count' (logizomai, G3049) for Adam's trespass even though he uses it 11 times across Romans 4 (4:3, 4:4, 4:5, 4:6, 4:8, 4:9, 4:10, 4:11, 4:22, 4:23, 4:24). The verb the federal-imputation reading would most want is present in the canon and absent from this paragraph, which is why the strict forensic-transfer form (legal courtroom transfer of guilt) remains underdetermined while 'to constitute' (kathistemi, G2525) in 5:19 only partially substitutes.

'The soul that sins shall die' (psyche he hamartanousa aute apothaneitai), a son does not bear the iniquity of the father. This Old Testament principle pulls against any reading in which guilt is mechanically transferred across generations. It is naturally read as governing judicial proceedings within Israel rather than the foundational anthropological situation (the underlying state of human nature) of the first man, but the lexical tension between this rule and a strict cross-generational imputation reading of Romans 5 is real, and is part of why the canon supplies two patterns the words do not rank.

Fathers shall not be put to death for children nor children for fathers, each shall die for his own sin. Same lexical principle as Ezekiel 18:20. Same resolution: it sets a judicial norm for human courts in Israel, while the Pauline universal-death-from-Adam of Romans 5:14 is the thing-to-be-explained that no purely individual-guilt model accounts for. The two principles coexist in the canon and the vocabulary does not tell the reader which frame governs the Adam case.

'Adam' (Adam, G0076) appears here, 'and Adam was not deceived' (kai Adam ouk epatethe), but the woman being deceived came into 'transgression' (parabasis, G3847). This is one of only nine canon occurrences of 'Adam' (Adam) and it locates primary responsibility with Adam without using any covenant-head or federal vocabulary. It supports Adam's representative weight but, like the anchor passages, names no mechanism, so it neither settles nor unsettles the federal-versus-seminal-versus-analogy question.

variant_units_examined.note: Indicative future 'we shall bear' (phoresomen, a simple statement about a future event) versus aorist subjunctive (a completed-action form used here as a 'let us' urging) hortatory 'let us bear' (phoresomen) is a real variant with strong external support for the subjunctive but adopted as indicative in most critical editions. It affects only the mood (whether the verb is a statement or an urging) of bearing the image of the heavenly man, not the Adam-Christ headship verdict.
Some witnesses add 'the Lord' (ho kyrios) after 'the second man from heaven'. Critical editions omit. The addition does not affect the 'first' (protos) and 'second' (deuteros) two-head structure.

A small minority omits 'not' (me) in 'over those who did not sin' (epi tous me hamartesantas). Without 'not' (me) the sense becomes those who did sin in Adam's likeness, removing the strongest internal hint that death reaches non-statutory-violators (those who never broke an explicit written command). The critical text retains 'not' (me) so the default reading stands, but if the variant were adopted the corporate-transmission case would weaken. This is a sub-question detail, not a flip of the disputed verdict.

variants.note: All anchor verses are New Testament and outside the CBGM-published (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, the formal manuscript-relationship method) 3 John scope, so this is 'ecm-shadow' (under the shadow of the Editio Critica Maior textual project). Variant judgments rely on Nestle-Aland and SBLGNT apparatus (the standard critical Greek New Testament editions), not on a published ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) for these books.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Adam as covenant-representative by appointment, so his one act is reckoned to those he represents. Takes 'because/in whom' (eph' ho) of Romans 5:12 with 'one man' (henos anthropou) as antecedent or as cause-in-Adam, treats 'they were constituted sinners' (katestathesan hamartoloi) in 5:19 as forensic constitution of status (a legal placement into a category by court ruling), and reads 'through one trespass to all men for condemnation' (di' henos paraptomatos eis pantas anthropous eis katakrima) as a juridical transaction strictly parallel to the one righteous act reckoned to the many. Its strongest lexical footing is the dense forensic vocabulary 'condemnation' (katakrima), 'judgment' (krima), and 'righteous verdict' (dikaioma) plus the 'appoint' sense of 'to constitute' (kathistemi).

Reads 'because/in whom all sinned' (eph' ho pantes hemarton) as all actually sinned in Adam because all humanity was naturally or biologically present in him, and reads 'in Adam' (en to Adam) in 1 Corinthians 15:22 as real ontological inclusion (real-being-included, not merely legal) rather than legal representation. It reaches the same universal liability rooted in one man but by participation in his nature rather than by an appointed legal headship. Its strongest lexical footing is the incorporative 'in' (en) plus dative (the 'to/in X' grammatical form) and the absence of any explicit covenant or appointment term.

Reads the whole comparison as a 'type, pattern' (typos, G5179) analogy: Adam's act sets in motion a sphere of sin and death that conditions his descendants, and Christ inaugurates the opposite sphere, without a transfer of personal guilt. It honors the explicit one-to-many structure and the type language while declining the forensic-transfer specification (the specifically courtroom-style guilt transfer). Its strongest lexical footing is 'type of the one to come' (typos tou mellontos) and the 'likeness' (homoioma) language of 5:14, plus the silence of 'to credit or count' (logizomai) in the paragraph.

Holds that corruption is transmitted naturally from Adam and that liability follows from the inherited corruption which produces actual sin, locating the legal moment downstream of Adam's own act rather than in a direct imputation (direct legal crediting) of it. It accepts the one-to-many transmission the text makes explicit but reads 'to constitute' (kathistemi) and the 'because/in whom' (eph' ho) clause as describing a derived, not immediate, constitution as sinners.

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical bundle anchors the Adam-Christ one-and-many parallelism cleanly and pan-passage (across all the anchor passages), but adjudication among the named lenses turns on the dual morphology (two possible grammatical readings) of 'because/in whom' (eph' ho) in Romans 5:12, on the 'appoint-versus-impute' range of 'to constitute' (kathistemi) in 5:19, and on the absence of 'to credit or count' (logizomai) from the paragraph. None of these is settled by the vocabulary alone, so each lens is recorded in its strongest lexical form.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Scripture pairs Adam and Christ as representative figures whose single acts have corporate consequence for those associated with them, and names Adam a type of the one to come. The precise mechanism by which Adam's transgression reaches his descendants, whether by covenant-representative appointment, natural or seminal participation, or analogy of influence, is the disputed specification.
stem_audit.notes: The words 'covenant' and 'federal head' and 'imputed' in the question stem encode a specific representative-headship taxonomy (a way of classifying head-of-the-people positions) and its forensic (courtroom-style) mechanism, neither of which the Greek of the anchor texts names of Adam. The underlying biblical claim, that one man's act reaches many and that Adam is the type of Christ, is explicit and broadly held. The narrower federal-imputation form is the contested part. The verdict is derived on the original stem and remains disputed, unchanged from the prior file.

lay_summary: Paul builds an unmistakable one-to-many parallel between Adam and Christ in Romans 5:12-19 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. The Greek hammers on 'through one man' (di' henos anthropou), set against 'the many' (hoi polloi), and locks the two halves together with the matched pair 'just as' (hosper) and 'so also' (houtos). Through one man sin entered the world and death through sin, and through one man Jesus Christ the gift comes to many. In 1 Corinthians 15:22 the preposition 'in' (en) frames two corporate humanities: in Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive. Paul even calls Adam a 'type or pattern' (typos) of the one to come. The strongest single verb is 'they were constituted' or 'were placed in a category' (katestathesan) in Romans 5:19, which elsewhere most often means appointed or set in place. So the many were placed in the category of sinners through one disobedience and will be placed in the category of righteous through one obedience. The forensic (courtroom-style) words 'judgment' (krima), 'condemnation' (katakrima), and 'righteous verdict' (dikaioma) add a judicial tone. So the words clearly establish that one man's act reaches many and that Adam stands as the counterpart to Christ. What the words do not do is name how. They never call Adam a covenant or federal head. The crux phrase 'because/in whom all sinned' (eph' ho pantes hemarton) in Romans 5:12 is built from 'on/upon' (epi) plus a relative pronoun, so it can mean 'because all sinned' or 'in whom all sinned', and Greek alone cannot decide. Tellingly, the precise reckoning verb 'to credit or count' (logizomai) that Paul repeats again and again in Romans 4 never appears in this Adam paragraph. Because of that gap, a representative-by-appointment reading, a we-were-all-in-him-by-nature reading, and an analogy-of-influence reading all fit the same text. The structural claim is supported, but the strict federal-imputation form (the specific legal-crediting form) is left open by the vocabulary, and that is why faithful readers diverge.
